issues.legal_issue: A restricted life interest granted by will to a female Hindu in the testator’s self-acquired property, independently of any pre-existing right, is not enlarged into absolute ownership when the will creates that interest for the first time.
material_facts: The house was the testator’s self-acquired property, which he owned exclusively.

By will, the testator gave the house’s ground and first floors to his son and daughter, respectively, as their absolute property, while giving his wife only a right to reside in the house during her lifetime and use its rental income for her maintenance and the house’s upkeep.
The wife’s interest was granted for the first time by the will and was not given in recognition or satisfaction of a pre-existing right.
The testator gave other property to his wife absolutely, and she did not seek maintenance from him.
The lower courts held that the wife’s interest remained a life interest under Section 14(2) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956; the appeal challenged that conclusion.
issues.conclusion: The wife’s life interest fell under Section 14(2) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 and remained a restricted estate until her death; it was not enlarged into absolute ownership under Section 14(1). The appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, a female Hindu’s limited interest in property held in recognition of a pre-existing right may enlarge into absolute ownership. Section 14(2) applies where a will or other instrument creates a new interest for the first time and expressly restricts it. Section 30 permits a Hindu to dispose of property by will, including by granting only a life interest. V. Tulasamma v. Sesha Reddy explains the distinction between a grant recognizing a pre-existing right and one creating a new restricted interest; Sadhu Singh v. Gurudwara Sahib Narike applies that distinction to a testamentary grant of a restricted interest. The Court also relied on the principles in Gullapalli Krishna Das v. Vishnumolakayya Venkayya, Bai Vajia v. Thakorbhai Chelabhai, and Thota Sesharathamma v. Thota Manikyamma in noting that the interpretation in V. Tulasamma had been consistently upheld.

rule.if: appeal_from_limited_estate_ruling and female_hindu_received_property_under_will and testator_owned_property_exclusively and will_created_new_interest_without_satisfying_preexisting_right and will_limited_interest_to_lifetime

predicates.appeal_from_limited_estate_ruling: A party appealed a ruling that an interest granted to a female beneficiary remained limited.
predicates.female_hindu_received_property_under_wil: A female Hindu received an interest in property under a will.
predicates.testator_owned_property_exclusively: The person making the will owned the property exclusively.
predicates.will_created_new_interest_without_satisf: The will granted the female beneficiary an interest for the first time rather than recognizing or satisfying a right she already had.
predicates.will_limited_interest_to_lifetime: The will restricted the female beneficiary’s interest to her lifetime.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns a limited-interest ruling and a female Hindu receives, under a will, a newly created lifetime interest in property owned exclusively by the testator, that interest remains restricted and is not enlarged.
